notes:
Temperature scales

  • $\dfrac{C}{5} = \dfrac{F-32}{9} = \dfrac{K-273}{5}$. Absolute zero $= 0$ K $= -273.15^\circ$C.

Thermal expansion

TypeFormula
Linear$L = L_0(1+\alpha\Delta T)$
Areal (superficial)$A = A_0(1+\beta\Delta T)$, $\beta = 2\alpha$
Volume (cubical)$V = V_0(1+\gamma\Delta T)$, $\gamma = 3\alpha$
  • Water shows anomalous expansion: density is maximum at $4^\circ$C; it contracts on heating from 0°C to 4°C and expands above 4°C.

Calorimetry

  • Heat $Q = mc\Delta T$ (specific heat $c$, unit J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$); molar specific heat $C = Q/(n\Delta T)$.
  • Latent heat: $Q = mL$. Water: $L_{fusion} = 3.34\times10^5$ J kg$^{-1}$ (0°C), $L_{vap} = 2.26\times10^6$ J kg$^{-1}$ (100°C). No temperature change during a phase change.
  • Principle of calorimetry: heat lost by hot body = heat gained by cold body (in an insulated system).

Heat transfer

ModeKey law
Conduction$\dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{KA(T_1-T_2)}{L}$; thermal conductivity $K$; no medium motion.
ConvectionHeat transfer by actual movement of fluid particles.
RadiationNo medium needed; travels as EM waves at speed of light.
  • For rods of same dimensions, thermal resistance $R = L/(KA)$ adds in series ($R=R_1+R_2$) and combines as $1/R=1/R_1+1/R_2$ in parallel.

Radiation laws

  • Stefan-Boltzmann law: energy radiated per unit area per unit time $E = \sigma T^4$ (black body); for a body with emissivity $e$: $E = e\sigma T^4$.
  • Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling $\propto$ (temperature of body $-$ surrounding temperature), valid for small temperature differences.
  • Wien's displacement law: $\lambda_m T = b$ (constant); a hotter body radiates its peak intensity at a shorter wavelength.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 2 questions from this chapter — one on thermal expansion or calorimetry (mixture numericals) and one on Stefan's law/Newton's law of cooling or conduction. Watch for unit consistency and remember $\beta=2\alpha$, $\gamma=3\alpha$.

questions.q: A temperature of 100°C on the Fahrenheit scale corresponds to
0 K on the Kelvin scale corresponds to
questions.explanation: Absolute zero (0 K) is $-273.15^\circ$C by definition of the Kelvin scale.

questions.q: A metal rod of length 2 m and coefficient of linear expansion $2\times10^{-5}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ is heated through 50°C. The increase in length is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L = L_0\alpha\Delta T = 2\times2\times10^{-5}\times50 = 2\times10^{-3}$ m $=2$ mm.

questions.q: If the coefficient of linear expansion of a material is $\alpha$, its coefficient of cubical (volume) expansion is
questions.explanation: For small expansions $\gamma = 3\alpha$ (and $\beta = 2\alpha$ for area).

questions.q: As water is cooled from 10°C to 0°C, its volume
questions.explanation: Water shows anomalous expansion: it contracts on cooling from 10°C to 4°C (density rising to a maximum at 4°C) and then expands as it is cooled further from 4°C to 0°C.

questions.q: 500 g of water at 20°C is heated to 80°C. If the specific heat of water is 4200 J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, the heat required is
questions.explanation: $Q = mc\Delta T = 0.5\times4200\times60 = 126000$ J $= 126$ kJ.

questions.q: The heat required to convert 10 g of ice at 0°C completely into water at 0°C (latent heat of fusion of ice $=3.34\times10^5$ J kg$^{-1}$) is
questions.explanation: $Q = mL = 0.01\times3.34\times10^5 = 3340$ J. No temperature change occurs during melting.

questions.q: 100 g of water at 90°C is mixed with 100 g of water at 10°C. Assuming no heat loss, the final temperature of the mixture is
questions.explanation: Equal masses of the same liquid: heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water, so final temperature is the simple average $=(90+10)/2 = 50^\circ$C.

questions.q: 50 g of ice at 0°C is mixed with 50 g of water at 80°C (specific heat of water $=1$ cal g$^{-1}$°C$^{-1}$, latent heat of fusion of ice $=80$ cal g$^{-1}$). The final temperature of the mixture is
questions.explanation: Heat needed to melt ice $=50\times80=4000$ cal. Heat available if water cools from 80°C to 0°C $=50\times1\times80=4000$ cal, exactly enough to melt all the ice with nothing left to raise temperature further, so the mixture settles at 0°C.

questions.q: Two metal rods of the same length and area of cross-section but thermal conductivities $K$ and $2K$ are joined end to end (in series) between two heat reservoirs. In the steady state, the temperature gradient is
options: twice as large in the rod of conductivity $K$
twice as large in the rod of conductivity $2K$
questions.explanation: In steady state the same heat current flows through both; $\dfrac{dT}{dx} \propto \dfrac1K$, so the rod with conductivity $K$ has twice the temperature gradient of the rod with conductivity $2K$.

questions.q: Heat transfer that occurs without any medium, purely by electromagnetic waves, is called
questions.explanation: Radiation is the only mode of heat transfer that can occur through vacuum, as electromagnetic waves.

questions.q: The energy radiated per second per unit area by a black body is proportional to
questions.explanation: Stefan-Boltzmann law: $E = \sigma T^4$.

questions.q: A black body at absolute temperature $T$ radiates energy at a rate $E$. If its temperature is doubled, the new rate of radiation is
questions.explanation: $E \propto T^4$, so doubling $T$ increases $E$ by a factor of $2^4 = 16$.

questions.q: Wien's displacement law states that $\lambda_m T = $ constant. This implies that as the temperature of a black body increases, the wavelength at which it radiates maximum energy
questions.explanation: Since $\lambda_m T$ is constant, $\lambda_m \propto 1/T$; a hotter body has its peak emission shifted to a shorter wavelength (e.g. from red to blue-white).

questions.q: Newton's law of cooling is applicable when
options: the temperature difference between body and surroundings is large
the body is a perfect black body only
the temperature difference between body and surroundings is small
questions.explanation: Newton's law of cooling (rate of loss of heat $\propto$ excess temperature over surroundings) is an approximation valid only for small temperature differences.

questions.q: A body cools from 60°C to 50°C in 10 minutes when the surrounding temperature is 30°C. By Newton's law of cooling, the average rate of fall of temperature depends on
options: the absolute temperature of the body only
the excess of average body temperature over surrounding temperature
the specific heat of the surroundings
the mass of the body only
questions.explanation: Newton's law of cooling states the rate of cooling is proportional to the difference between the (average) body temperature and the surrounding temperature.

questions.q: A bimetallic strip made of brass and iron (brass having a higher coefficient of linear expansion) bends towards the iron side on heating because
options: brass expands more than iron, so the strip curves with brass on the outside
questions.explanation: On heating, brass (higher $\alpha$) elongates more than iron, forcing the strip to curve with brass forming the outer (longer) arc, i.e. the strip bends towards the iron side.

questions.q: The SI unit of thermal conductivity $K$ is
questions.explanation: From $Q/t = KA\Delta T/L$, $K = \dfrac{Q L}{t A \Delta T}$, giving units W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ = J s$^{-1}$m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$.

questions.q: The triple point of water, used to define the Kelvin temperature scale, occurs at
questions.explanation: By international agreement, the triple point of water (where ice, water and water vapour coexist in equilibrium) is assigned the value 273.16 K exactly.

questions.q: A liquid has a real (absolute) coefficient of cubical expansion of $180\times10^{-6}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ and is held in a glass vessel of cubical expansion coefficient $27\times10^{-6}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$. The apparent coefficient of expansion of the liquid observed in this vessel is
questions.explanation: $\gamma_{apparent} = \gamma_{real} - \gamma_{vessel} = 180\times10^{-6}-27\times10^{-6}=153\times10^{-6}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$.

questions.q: A square metal plate of side 1 m at 20°C has $\alpha = 2\times10^{-5}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$. When heated to 120°C, the increase in its area is
questions.explanation: $\beta=2\alpha=4\times10^{-5}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$; $\Delta A=A_0\beta\Delta T=1\times4\times10^{-5}\times100=4\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$.

questions.q: Small gaps are deliberately left between successive segments of a railway track. This is to
options: reduce the material cost of laying the track
improve friction for wheels rolling on the track
allow room for thermal expansion in hot weather and avoid buckling of the rails
questions.explanation: Metal rails expand on heating in summer; the gaps provide room for this expansion and prevent the track from buckling.

questions.q: Invar (an iron-nickel alloy) is used in making precision pendulum clocks and measuring tapes mainly because it has
options: very low (nearly zero) coefficient of linear expansion
very high coefficient of linear expansion
questions.explanation: Invar's very small $\alpha$ means its length barely changes with temperature, keeping measurements and pendulum periods accurate despite temperature fluctuations.

questions.q: A calorimeter of water equivalent 20 g contains 180 g of water at 25°C (specific heat of water $=1$ cal g$^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$). The total heat required to raise the temperature of the calorimeter and water together to 35°C is
questions.explanation: Water equivalent accounts for the calorimeter's own heat capacity as if it were extra water; effective mass $=180+20=200$ g, so $Q=200\times1\times10=2000$ cal.

questions.q: The heat required to convert 5 g of water at 100°C completely into steam at 100°C (latent heat of vaporisation of water $=2.26\times10^6$ J kg$^{-1}$) is

Two rods of the same material, length and temperature difference across their ends, but cross-sectional areas $A$ and $2A$, conduct heat independently in parallel between the same hot and cold reservoirs. The ratio of the heat currents through them (thinner : thicker) is
questions.explanation: Heat current $=KA\Delta T/L \propto A$ for fixed $K,L,\Delta T$, so the ratio of currents equals the ratio of areas, $A:2A=1:2$.

questions.q: The heat capacity of a body and the specific heat capacity of its material differ in that
options: heat capacity has SI units of J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$
they are always numerically identical for any object
specific heat capacity depends on the object's mass, while heat capacity does not
heat capacity is an extensive property (depends on mass), equal to $mc$, while specific heat capacity is an intensive property of the material alone
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity $c$ is a per-unit-mass material property, while the heat capacity of a particular body is $mc$, which scales with the amount of substance present.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes evaporation from boiling?
options: Both occur at exactly the same temperature and by the same mechanism
Evaporation occurs at all temperatures from the liquid's free surface only, while boiling occurs at a fixed temperature throughout the bulk of the liquid, forming bubbles
Boiling occurs only in vacuum, while evaporation requires atmospheric pressure
Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point, while boiling can occur at any temperature
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that occurs at any temperature, whereas boiling occurs throughout the liquid's volume (via bubble formation) only at a fixed temperature determined by the external pressure.

questions.q: A pressure cooker cooks food faster than an open pan mainly because
options: the cooker material has unusually high thermal conductivity
increasing pressure inside lowers the boiling point of water, so it boils at a lower temperature and cooks faster
the sealed lid increases the specific heat of water
increasing pressure inside raises the boiling point of water, so cooking occurs at a higher temperature
questions.explanation: Boiling point rises with increasing pressure; the sealed cooker traps steam, raising the internal pressure and hence the temperature at which water boils, cooking food faster.

questions.q: Regelation is the phenomenon in which ice, under increased pressure, melts at a temperature below 0°C and refreezes once the pressure is removed. This is possible because
options: regelation only occurs in a vacuum
ice always melts at exactly 0°C regardless of pressure
water is denser than ice, so increased pressure favours the liquid (lower-volume) phase, lowering the melting point
pressure has no effect on the melting point of ice
questions.explanation: Ice's anomalous behaviour (water being denser than ice) means applied pressure favours melting, lowering the melting point slightly — the ice refreezes once the pressure is released and it recools.

questions.q: Using Wien's displacement law ($\lambda_m T = b = 2.9\times10^{-3}$ m K), the wavelength at which the Sun (surface temperature $\approx5800$ K) radiates maximum energy is approximately
questions.explanation: $\lambda_m = b/T = (2.9\times10^{-3})/5800 \approx 5\times10^{-7}$ m $= 500$ nm, in the visible range, consistent with the Sun appearing yellow-white.

questions.q: Two spheres A and B of the same material have radii in the ratio 1:2 and surface temperatures in the ratio 2:1. The ratio of the total power radiated by them, $P_A:P_B$, is
questions.explanation: $P=e\sigma(4\pi r^2)T^4 \propto r^2T^4$. $\dfrac{P_A}{P_B}=\dfrac{1^2\times2^4}{2^2\times1^4}=\dfrac{16}{4}=4$, so $P_A:P_B=4:1$.

questions.q: The emissivity $e$ of a surface, used in $E=e\sigma T^4$, satisfies
options: $0\le e\le1$, with $e=1$ for a perfect black body
$e$ can exceed 1 for shiny polished surfaces
$e$ is always exactly 1 for every real surface
questions.explanation: Emissivity is a dimensionless ratio comparing a surface's emission to that of an ideal black body at the same temperature, so $0\le e\le1$, with $e=1$ only for a perfect black body.

questions.q: On a graph of temperature versus heat supplied to a solid being converted to liquid and then to vapour, the flat (horizontal) portions of the graph correspond to
options: phase changes (melting or boiling), where all the supplied heat goes into latent heat with no temperature change
periods when no heat is being supplied at all
the specific heat of the substance becoming zero
questions.explanation: During a phase change, supplied heat is used entirely to break/form intermolecular bonds (latent heat), so the temperature stays constant even as heat continues to flow in.

questions.q: The heat required to convert 100 g of ice at 0°C into water at 20°C is (latent heat of fusion of ice $=3.34\times10^5$ J kg$^{-1}$, specific heat of water $=4200$ J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: Melting: $Q_1=mL=0.1\times3.34\times10^5=33400$ J. Heating: $Q_2=mc\Delta T=0.1\times4200\times20=8400$ J. Total $=41800$ J $=41.8$ kJ.

questions.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales give the same numerical reading?
questions.explanation: Setting $C=F=x$ in $C=\dfrac{5}{9}(F-32)$ gives $x=\dfrac59(x-32) \Rightarrow 9x=5x-160 \Rightarrow x=-40$.

questions.q: The specific heat capacity of a gas is 700 J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ and its molar mass is 0.028 kg mol$^{-1}$ (e.g. nitrogen). Its molar specific heat capacity is
questions.explanation: Molar specific heat $C=Mc=0.028\times700=19.6$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$.

questions.q: A metal cube of side 10 cm ($\alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$) is heated through 100°C. The increase in its volume is approximately
questions.explanation: $V_0=1000$ cm$^3$; $\gamma=3\alpha=3.6\times10^{-5}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$; $\Delta V=V_0\gamma\Delta T=1000\times3.6\times10^{-5}\times100=3.6$ cm$^3$.

questions.q: A steel rod of cross-sectional area $2\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$ is fixed rigidly between two supports. Taking $Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa and $\alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$, the compressive force developed in the rod when its temperature rises by 40°C is
questions.explanation: Since the rod cannot expand, the would-be strain converts entirely to stress: $F=YA\alpha\Delta T=2\times10^{11}\times2\times10^{-4}\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times40=1.92\times10^4$ N.

questions.q: According to Kirchhoff's law of radiation, a surface that is a good absorber of thermal radiation at a given temperature is also
options: a good emitter of radiation at that temperature
a poor emitter of radiation at that temperature
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's law states that the emissivity of a surface at a given temperature equals its absorptivity at that temperature, so good absorbers (like black surfaces) are also good emitters.
